idiom_name: struct/enum core + pure methods; a small class holds state and does the IO
implementation_notes: Put the decisions in `struct`/`enum` value types with pure methods or free functions (`let` bindings, `Result`, enums with associated values for outcomes) and keep the effects in a small `final class` that holds the value and implements networking, persistence and IO - the Swift shape of the pattern: encapsulate the logic in value types with pure functions, and use objects only to store those values and provide side effects. Because structs are copied on assignment and `mutating` methods produce new values, the core cannot share state with the shell; reference-type members and captured closures are the leak. A protocol-injected Core class is only needed where the core must call out, which is what the pattern removes.
pitfalls: A `struct` holding a `class` (or a closure that captures one) is not isolated: copies share the reference, so mutation through it is an invisible effect - keep reference types out of the core's stored properties.
`Date()`, `UUID()` and `Task { }` inside the core make it impure and non-deterministic; pass the date/time in (as `finish(at:)` does) and let the shell start the tasks.
`@MainActor`, `ObservableObject` and dispatch queues belong to the shell: core code that touches them cannot be tested synchronously and drags UI concerns into the rules.

variants.name: Reducer + middleware (unidirectional flow)
variants.idiom_name: Reducer<State, Action> core; @MainActor Store + Middleware effects
variants.implementation_notes: The opinionated form: the core is a `Reducer` (`(State, Action) -> State`) and the shell is a `@MainActor` store that publishes the state, applies the reducer, and runs `Middleware` closures that perform the IO and feed back a new action; effects run in a `TaskGroup`, so they are parallel and cooperatively cancellable, and the store holds the dependencies. The reducer stays synchronous and testable by calling it with a state and an action, which is why reducers work so well as the functional core in UI applications. Choose it when the application state is shared and long-lived; for a single entry point the small store of the other variant is enough.
pitfalls: Middleware runs after the reducer, so an action produced by a middleware that is itself intercepted can loop forever - keep 'internal' actions (status updates) out of the middleware's switch.
Effects started with a detached `Task` escape the store's lifetime (and the view's); use the structured `TaskGroup` so cancellation propagates when the store goes away.
`@Published` state mutation off the main actor is a data race: the store must stay `@MainActor` and the reducer must never touch it, which means middleware may only return actions.
